newsitem.title: USA: Stocks not seen at start of major reversal. [CORRECTED 08:41 GMT 9/8]
newsitem.headline: Stocks not seen at start of major reversal. [CORRECTED 08:41 GMT 9/8]

text.p: Stocks might see some follow-through selling early next week but do not appear to be at the start of a major reversal, analysts said.

Spooked by a steep rise in long-term interest rates, stocks sold off sharply Friday, but analysts said there has not been the sort of fundamental shift in the outlook for interest rates or corporate profits to cripple Wall Street's bull market.

The Dow Jones industrial average slumped 156.78 points, or nearly 2 percent, to close at 8,031.22. It was down as much as 211.6 points during the day.(Corrects figure from 206 points to 211.6 points.)
The downdraft was triggered by a sell-off in the bond market that drove the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond to 6.64 percent Friday, up from 6.53 percent on Thursday.
Analysts said that greater concern about growth in the U.S. economy -- and subsequent inflation -- would weigh on bonds in the near term.
But significant damage to stocks and bonds were unlikely unless inflation shows signs of kicking in, which it has yet to do, analysts said.

"The bond market continues to have an over-sensitivity to growth because it concludes growth creates inflation," said Thomas McManus, chief market strategist at NatWest Securities. "I don't think inflation is a problem."

McManus said that the long-bond yield could rise to 6.75 percent and the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks could dip to 900 as part of the current pullback, although he added stocks "could stabilise at any time."
The S&P 500 fell 17.65 points, or 1.8 percent, to 933.54.
The Dow hit a record closing high of 8,259.31 on Wednesday, up 29 percent from its closing low of 6,391.69 for this year hit April 11.
The rise has left stocks with very little room for news that does not fit into the "perfect world" scenario of steady growth and low inflation, analysts said.
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross, likened Friday's sell-off to a child realising the "Tooth Fairy" does not exist.
"It's not the end of the world," he said.
But analysts said there were some warning signs in Friday's action, including the broad reach of the sell-off. Losing issues outnumbered gainers by a five-to-one ratio on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The breadth was just awful today," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.

While Acuff called Friday's move "healthy profit-taking" following the market's recent rise, he said investors should expect further volatility as traders give extra scrutiny to upcoming economic data, including retail sales and producer price data on Wednesday and consumer price numbers on Thursday.
The key question is whether a major reversal of the recent trend of declining interest rates will set in, said Robert Walberg, chief equity analysts at Briefing.Com.

If the long-bond yield holds below 7.00 percent, a downturn of more than 500 points from the Dow peak is unlikely, Walberg said. "But if we're seeing a significant sea change in the bond market, it could get ugly for stocks."

But some analysts expressed confidence investors would continue their habit of using sell-offs as buying opportunities. "I think they buy the dips," said William LeFevre, senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
